en: The Wave of Bliss of Śiva.

May this prostration be offered in my heart to Śiva and Śivā— who are adorned with the crescent moon as their crest-ornament, who are the fruit of their own asceticism, who have manifested the fruits [of grace] for their devotees, who are the source of welfare for the three worlds in no small measure, who are ever-renewed, and whose experience flashes forth as bliss. May that river of Your deeds, O Śambhu, be victorious— it which flows down, shatters the dust of sin, and falls into the channels of the streams of wisdom.
Bestowing the pacification of the distress of wandering in saṃsāra, may the wave of auspicious bliss dwell within the lake of my heart.

I worship in my heart Śiva— the one to be known by the three Vedas, the beloved, the destroyer of Tripura, the primordial, the three-eyed, the noble one with his mass of matted hair, who wears a necklace of swaying serpents, the bearer of the deer, the Great God, the Lord who looks upon me with compassion, the Lord of Creatures, accompanied by Ambā, the refuge, and the one who utterly transcends all comparison.
Tens of thousands of gods exist in this world who bestow only meager fruits; neither in the midst of them nor even in a dream should one follow them or seek their rewards.
O Śambhu, O Śiva, O Śiva, I long beseech you for the worship of your lotus feet—a blessing difficult to attain even for those who dwell in the proximity of Hari, Brahmā, and the other gods.

Unskilled in memory, scripture, medicine, omens, poetry, song, or speech; unskilled in the Purāṇas, mantras, praise, dance, or laughter—how can there be favor from kings toward me? O Lord of Creatures, who am I? O All-Knowing One, protect me, a mere beast, with Your renowned compassion, O All-Pervading One!
Does a jar, or even a lump of clay, or a tiny speck of smoke, or fire, or a mountain, or a cloth, or even a thread, ever bring about the quelling of a terrible calamity?
In vain do you undergo the agitation of your throat with forceful words of logic; worship the lotus feet of Śambhu and attain supreme bliss, O wise one!

(6) May your mind dwell upon His lotus feet, your speech in the chanting of hymns, your hands in the act of worship, your hearing in the rite of listening to His stories, your intellect in meditation, and your pair of eyes in the manifestation of His form—by what other means, O Supreme Śiva, could I know the highest truth? (7)
Just as the intellect perceives silver in mother-of-pearl, a gem in glass or stone, milk in flour-water, and water in the mirages of a desert;
so too, O Paśupati, through divine delusion, the dull-witted person worships one other than You, the Great Lord of Gods, failing to recognize You within his own mind.
The dull-minded one wanders for the sake of flowers in a deep lake, in a desolate wilderness, in a terrible forest, and upon a vast mountain.
O Lord of Umā, having surrendered their single mind to you like a lotus, alas, people here do not know how to abide in happiness.
Whether it be humanhood, divinity, the state of a forest deer, a mosquito, a beast, an insect, or even the repeated birth as a bird—
if the heart is perpetually intent on sporting in the waves of supreme bliss from the remembrance of your lotus feet, then what is the use of this body?
Whether he be a student, a householder, an ascetic with matted hair, or any other man whatsoever—O Bhava, what does it matter who he is?
If this lotus of his heart is subject to you, O Paśupati, then you belong to him, O Śambhu, and you bear the burden of his worldly existence.
(11) Whether he dwells in a cave, a home, outside, in a forest, on a mountain peak, in water, or in fire—tell me, what fruit is there in one’s dwelling?
O Śambhu, if one’s inner organ is always fixed upon Your feet, he is a yogi, he is a supreme yogin, and he is truly happy.

In this essence-less saṃsāra, it is fitting for you, through your supreme grace, to protect me—who am blind, wandering with a dull intellect far from my own worship. O Paśupati, who else but you is so skilled in protecting the wretched? And who else in this entire world is a refuge other than yourself for one such as me?
O Lord of Creatures, you are indeed the master of the wretched and their supreme kinsman; I am the foremost among them, so how much more so are these two?
O Śiva, all my offenses must be forgiven by you alone, and you must strive to make me your own; this is the path of kinsmen.
If you do not disregard me, why do you snatch away from me the decree of fate—which turns one away from meditation on you and is filled with wicked hopes—if you are powerless [to change it]?
O Paśupati, that head of Vidhātṛ is indeed not well-rounded; for who could have disheveled it without effort, using only the tips of his fingernails?
(15) May Viriñci be long-lived! But you must protect those four heads of his; he, indeed, has inscribed wretchedness upon the earth.
O Śiva, what consideration protects me with pure compassion? For your glance itself is intent upon protecting the miserable. (16)

O Lord, whether it be due to the fruit of my merits or out of compassion for you, even though you are gracious toward me, how shall I behold the pair of your stainless lotus feet? The multitude of gods, filled with agitation, obscures them with their own crowns of gold and rubies. (17) You alone are the bestower of the supreme fruit for the worlds; bearing the divine path, those headed by Hari once again take refuge at your very root.
How great is your courtesy, O Śiva, and how vast is my hope? When indeed will you protect me with a gaze filled with compassion?

(18) In this worldly existence—which is full of wicked hopes, a mere door-bolt at the gate of the house of misfortune, difficult to traverse, an abode of sin, and a generator of suffering—why do you not dispel my weariness? For whose benefit should I speak? If you have affection for me, O Śiva, then we are truly ones who have achieved their life's purpose. (19)

O Lord Śiva, O All-pervading One, bind with firm devotion this exceedingly restless monkey of my heart— which always roams the forest of delusion, dances upon the mountain-peaks of young women's breasts, and instantly wanders at will in every direction— and make it dependent upon You.
[Make it] supported by the pillar of fortitude, bound with the cords of virtue, possessed of movement, variegated, rich in lotuses, and fashioned daily upon the path of the righteous.
O Enemy of Smara, O Lord Śiva, attended by your powers and your hosts, having reached this clear cloth-tent of my heart, be victorious along with your Śakti!
O Lord of Thieves, this thief of a mind, enslaved to seizing wealth through greed and other vices, is busily intent on entering the house of the wealthy and flits about in many ways;
how can I endure him here? O Śaṅkara, O All-pervading Lord, having brought this [thief] under your control, show mercy toward me, who am innocent. 22
"I perform this worship of you; O Lord, grant me happiness instantly! By performing it, you surely bestow upon her the fruits of the status of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, O Śaṅkara, O All-pervading One, how can I endure here the distress of wandering as a deer in heaven and on earth in order to behold you again?
Or when, on Kailāsa, in a palace of gold and jewels, shall I dwell with the Gaṇas before Śambhu, with my hands joined in a clear gesture of reverence?"
O All-pervading Lord Sāmba, O Supreme Śiva, crying out "Protect me!", I shall pass through eons of creation as if they were a mere moment in happiness.

When shall I behold you—the blue-throated one with three eyes, whose body is embraced by Umā, who holds a deer and a broken axe in his hands—standing upon the hump of the great bull lowing with rut, while being restrained by the hosts of Brahmā and others with hymns and cries of "Victory! Victory!", amidst their playful antics? Or when, O Lord of the Mountain, having seen you and grasped the beautiful lotus-like feet of your auspicious form with both hands, shall I bear them upon my head, my eyes, and my chest?
Embracing and smelling those fragrances of blooming lotuses, I shall experience joy in my heart through the two fires of incense and perfume.

(26) With the Golden Mountain (Meru) in my hand, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) standing near me, the hosts of celestial wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi) dwelling in my home, the cool-rayed moon upon my head, and all that is auspicious at my feet—what object could I possibly lack? Let my mind be devoted solely to your service.

O Śiva, O Mahādeva! By worshipping you, *sārūpya* (attainment of your form) is achieved; by chanting your names, *sāmīpya* (proximity) is attained through conversation with the company of those foremost among the people devoted to Śiva.

By meditating on your body, which consists of the moving and the non-moving, *sālokya* (residing in the same world) is reached, O Lord of Bhavānī; and here, *sāyujya* (union) is accomplished for me—O Master, I am one who has fulfilled his purpose.
I worship your lotus feet, I contemplate you, the Supreme, day after day; I go for refuge to you, the Lord, with my speech, and I entreat only you, O All-pervading One.
O Śambhu, Teacher of the World, bestow upon me your compassionate Cākṣuṣī vision, long prayed for through divine means; grant the instruction for the happiness of my mind.
O Viṣṇu, if there be in me the thousand-rayed nature in the act of producing garments, the nature of the wind in the offering of flowers,
the presiding authority of Agni in the cooking of food,
and the essence of gold within the vessel— then, O Lord whose crest-jewel is the young moon, O Paśupati, O Master and Teacher of the three worlds, may I perform service unto you.

O Lord of Beasts, though this [fire] is not capable of providing supreme benefit, you nevertheless behold with it the multitudes of moving and unmoving beings within your belly as well as those situated outside;
yet, though you have swallowed with your throat this terrifying poison—which is a supreme medicine for the flight of all immortals and a source of exceeding flames—you have not vomited it up at all.

O Great-souled Śambhu, tell me: how was that fierce poison, which causes terror to all the enemies of the gods, rendered harmless by you? Why was it held in your hand? Is it a ripe jambū fruit in your palm? Was it placed upon your tongue as a perfected pill (*siddhavaṭikā*), or is this blue jewel worn as an ornament around your neck? Please explain.
O Lord, for those like me, a single act of service, prostration, praise, worship, remembrance, listening to Your stories, or even a mere glance is not enough.
O Master, what can be gained by the toil of following unstable deities? What liberation is there from this [world], and if it exists, why would one need to pray for it?
What can we say of your audacity, O Paśupati? O Śambhu, who else possesses such fortitude as yours? And how could this state of yours be attained by others?
Beholding the hosts of gods falling away, the throngs of sages trembling, and the entire phenomenal world perishing in dissolution, you alone remain fearless, sporting in the density of bliss.

You are the sustainer of the welfare of all, the bestower of every auspiciousness upon the striving, the one who imparts knowledge of the seen and the unseen, and who pervades both the external and the internal.
O Śambhu, what should I understand of you, the omniscient one who acts out of compassion? I remember daily in my heart that you are my supreme inner self.

O Sāmba, having placed the pair of your lotus-feet within the jar of my mind—which is filled with the nectar of joy and enveloped by the quality of devotion—I utter the mantra of pure being (*sattva*), bringing about the purification of the house of my own body; thus proclaiming a "day of merit" (*puṇyāha*) and securing auspiciousness, I manifest the fruit of consciousness.

Having made the ocean of sacred tradition their churning rod with the mind as the handle, joined with the rope of firm devotion, and having churned it with great care, the assemblies of the wise—like so many gods—extracted the moon, the wish-fulfilling tree, the fragrant celestial cow, and the jewel of thought; they thus spread the nectar of eternal bliss and the constant good fortune of the Goddess of Fortune for the intelligent.

Śiva, who is the embodiment of nectar revealed by the mountain of prior merit, who is gracious, the moon, served by his excellent attendants, the bearer of the deer, full, and the liberator from darkness, [is the one who grants these].
When the mind is marked by lotuses, it becomes an ocean of bliss; then the activity of the flowers of the intellect unfolds with boldness.
My Dharma has four feet and is well-practiced; evil has come to destruction; lust, anger, pride, and the like have fallen away; and auspicious times have been manifested.
The great medicine of the bliss of knowledge has borne fine fruit while the Lord of Liberation—ever to be honored—remains as the crest-jewel of kings in the city of the lotus of the mind.

(39) And by means of the machine of the intellect, with the water-jars of speech and the succession of channels and sub-channels of poetry, the divine nectar from the ocean of the deeds of Sadāśiva has been brought forth.

O Lord, Master of the Universe, when those whose ears are joined to the field of the heart and who possess the measure of devotion spread success, how can there be fear for me, your servant, from famine?

For the sake of liberation from the arising of sin and for the attainment of radiant sovereignty, I have offered prayers with my tongue, mind, head, feet, hands, and ears through hymns to the Conqueror of Death (*mṛtyuñjaya*), meditation, prostrations, circumambulations, worship, sight, and hearing; therefore, command me, determine that for me, and do not speak anything other than to me alone.

With profundity as its moat, firm fortitude as its rampart, the rising multitude of virtues as its strength, the collection of wealth and senses as its gates, and knowledge as its abundance of provisions—O God who is ever dear to Durgā, please take up residence in my mind-fortress, which is thus equipped with every requisite.
O Lord Giriśa, do not wander here and there; O primordial Kirāta, dwell right here within me, on the very frontier of the forest of my mind.

Deer abound in great numbers—those who delight in intoxication, as well as envy, delusion, and the like; having slain them, you will obtain the reward desired by those who take pleasure in the sport of hunting.
With a deer held in his hand, the lord of elephants shattered, and the fierce tiger torn apart—Śiva, of radiant form and five-faced within the cavern of my heart, whence can there be fear at the end?

In this eternal tree of prosody, frequented by the best of birds (the meters) perched upon its branches, which bestows perpetual bliss, dispels weariness, and is illuminated by fruits that are showers of nectar; [in this tree...]
O crest-jewel of the bird-like mind, abandon this futile wandering; enough with others! Constantly sport in the nest formed by the pair of Śaṅkara’s lotus feet.

O royal swan of the mind, though you have been washed by the splendor of the beauty of rows of claws and by the rising majesty of nectar, and though you have been resorted to by flocks of swans in the lovely Padmarāga gem, remain within the palace of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain—the pair of his feet—and constantly engage in private, spontaneous dalliance with the throngs of the brides that are the various forms of devotion.

In the garden of the heart, which is frequented by the springtime of meditation upon Śambhu, there shine forth the withered leaves of sin; there flourish the clusters of the creeper of devotion, supported by the sprouts of merit;

there gleam the buds of virtue, the flowers of the words of recitation, the good latent impressions (*sadvāsanā*), the waves of the nectar-essence of the bliss of knowledge, and the exalted fruit of pure consciousness.

[47] [The mind] is the abode of the essence of eternal bliss, the refuge for the lotuses of the hearts of gods and sages, transparent, served by the virtuous twice-born, and manifested through the pure latent impressions of those whose hearts are free from defilement.
O swan adorned by the mind, go to the lake of meditation upon Śambhu; why endure the fatigue born of wandering through the puddles of inferior refuges?

May the creeper of devotion—filled with the nectar of bliss, rising from the basin around the lotus feet of Hara, provided with branches and sub-branches, stainless, and having climbed high over the mass of clouds that are the body of the lofty mind—become the bestower of my eternal desired fruits, nurtured by virtuous deeds.

I worship the great Liṅga of Mallikārjuna on Śrīparvata, embraced by Śivā; it unfolds at the commencement of twilight, is established in various locations within the Upaniṣads (the head of the Vedas), is delightful to the bees of those filled with love, is repeatedly adorned by virtuous impressions (*sadvāsanā*), is bedecked with the lord of serpents as its ornament, is worthy of worship by all the gods, is manifested through its attributes, and is embraced by Śivā.

May that Lord who dwells on Śrīśaila— the one who sports with the horned goddess, who is fierce in his dancing, who seizes the ichor of elephants, who brings joy to Mādhava, who resounds with sound, whose body is of great whiteness, who is honored by the five-arrowed god of love, who possesses noble wings, and who wanders through the groves of flowers— may he, the sovereign lord, sport as a king of bees within the lotus of my heart’s desire.

O Blue-throated Śambhu, my mind, like a cātaka bird, ever longs for you— who rains down the nectar of compassion, who is skilled in dispelling the summer heat of dense calamities, whose form fulfills desires, who is to be cultivated by the virtuous-minded for the arising of the fruit of the crop of knowledge, and who is the mountain-dweller upon whom the peacock of devotion dances with its crest of quivering matted locks.

I worship that Blue-throated One (Nīlakaṇṭha), who is praised as a fire by his crest, as a peacock by his eyes, and as a cuckoo by the cries of his instruction in the *praṇava* for those prostrate before him;
who, seeing the dark, mountain-born Śyāmā of cloud-like luster, dances with joy in the pleasure-grove of Vedānta.

The end of the day of the twilight-dharma, the manifold sounds produced by the strikes of Hari’s hands, the thundering of the clouds in the sky, and the flickering glances of the gods—these are [the omens].
I worship that Nīlamaṇṭha, where the rain of the spreading tears of joy from devotees is like a peahen’s downpour, and where the auspicious, brilliant *tāṇḍava* dance prevails.

To the primordial one, of immeasurable splendor, who is to be known through the words of the Vedas, who is the goal to be attained, whose self consists of knowledge and bliss, who is ever-exerting himself for the protection of the three worlds,

who is the object of meditation for all yogis, who is praised by the hosts of gods, who possesses the power of illusion, who is perfectly absorbed in the cosmic egg, who wears matted locks— to that Śambhu, this prostration is offered.

This [world] does not belong to Śambhu, who is eternal, whose essence consists of the three *guṇas*, the conqueror of the cities, the source of prosperity for Kātyāyanī, the Truth, the primordial progenitor, the embodiment of consciousness directly perceived by the minds of sages, the creator of the three worlds through *māyā*, the one who moves within the conclusion of all the Vedas, and who wears matted hair during the fervor of his evening dance.
(56) O Lord, I wander in vain, seeking wealth from everyone for the sake of constantly filling my own belly; I do not know how to serve you.
O Śarva, it is surely by the power of the ripening of my merit from previous births that You abide within all; therefore, O Paśupati, I am one who must be protected by You.
The single friend of the lotus, having pierced the sphere of darkness pervading the earth and sky, becomes an object of sight; yet you possess the radiance of ten million suns.
O Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), why are you not perceived? Alas, how dense must my ignorance be! Having dispelled all of that for me, be gracious before my very eyes.
When the swan desires the lotus forest, the *cātaka* bird the dark rain-cloud, the ruddy goose the moon which is dear to the *kokanada* lily, and likewise the *cakora* bird the moon day after day;
so too, O Lord Paśupati, my mind yearns for Your pair of lotus feet—the goal sought by those on the path of consciousness, O All-pervading One, Lord of Gaurī, which bestow the bliss of liberation.

As a traveler on a riverbank exhausted by the toil of carrying water seeks the shade of a tree; as a weary guest fears the rain and seeks the home of a householder; as one distressed by darkness seeks a lamp; and as one shivering with cold seeks a fire—so do you, O mind, abandon all fear and go happily to the lotus feet of Śambhu, which remove every dread.

Just as the *akolla* seed reaches its own progeny, the magnet stone the iron, the needle the skilled artisan, the creeper its own lordly tree, and the ocean the beloved river, so too does the movement of the mind reach the pair of lotus-feet of Paśupati and remain there forever; that is called devotion (*bhakti*).

With tears of joy she spreads a covering of horripilation; through her purity she provides a veil; with the presence of her voice at the mouth of the conch she fills its interior; and with the nectar of her conduct she provides nourishment for the belly.
O Lord, having seated the child-like devotee upon the couch of meditation, Devotion—the mother who generates devotion—protects him by means of Rudrākṣa beads and sacred ash as armor for his body.
The sandal worn on the path becomes the foot-stool for the body of the Lord of Creatures; the rinsing water from His mouth becomes a divine consecration for the Enemy of the Cities;
even a morsel of meat remaining from what was slightly eaten becomes a fresh offering—alas, what does devotion not transform? Indeed, the forest-dweller becomes the crest-jewel of devotion.

Beating the chest of Death, crushing the hard fits of epilepsy, wandering over mountains, and rubbing against the millions of crowns of bowing gods—O Śambhu, is such an act appropriate for Your pair of feet, so tender? Please always grant me the privilege of walking upon the jeweled sandals of Your heart.
Fearing a blow to his chest, Vaivasvata (Yama) trembles; the gods perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) with the lamp-flames of the jewels shining from their crowns.

O Lord of Bhavānī, for one whose mind performs worship at your lotus feet, what is difficult to obtain in this world? Seeing [such a devotee], the bride Liberation (*muktivadhū*) offers him a secret embrace.

For the sake of sport, you create the entire universe, and those people are your play-animals (*krīḍāmṛga*); my performance of action is performed by me for your pleasure alone. 65. For one whose mind performs worship at your lotus feet—[a mind] which, fearing a blow to the chest, causes Vaivasvata to tremble, while the gods perform the *nīrājana* with the lamp-flames of the jewels blazing from their crowns, and which the bride Liberation embraces closely upon seeing—it, O Lord of Bhavānī, what is difficult to obtain here? For the sake of sport, you create the entire manifold universe, and those people are your play-animals; the performance of my own karma is indeed for your pleasure.
O Śambhu, my conduct was certainly intended to provoke your curiosity; therefore, O Paśupati, you must surely provide me with protection.

(66) I attain that supreme state of eternal bliss, which is the beautiful ground of enjoyment marked by thrills of joy and a flood of tears from manifold satisfaction, and which is served by those longing for the fruit of the eternal state. (67)

O compassionate Lord of Creatures, protect my one cow of devotion, which constantly yields the nectar of immeasurable joy, dwells upon the pure udder of Your feet, and has reached the ripening of great merit.
O God, dullness, beastliness, blemish, and crooked conduct do not exist in me.

O crest-jewel of kings, if you exist, am I not a worthy recipient of your ornament? (69) It is fitting that you, whose form is gracious and easily accessible, should be honored by me in private with a mind free from constraint;
for within my heart dwells Rājaśekhara, my lord, who bestows rewards beyond counting and is superior even to the world. (70)

Having conquered the enemies that are his sins with the unerring volleys of arrows consisting of the remembrance of Śiva— discharged from the bow of his inner being, which is bent by the quality of ascended devotion— the victorious lord of wise men brings forth the stable royal fortune of bliss.
Having perceived the region of darkness with the collyrium of meditation and having pierced it with the powerful mantras of the Lord’s names, [he attains the light].
O Śiva, those who bear here upon their heads Your lotus feet, which rest upon the divine [crown] and are adorned by serpents, have achieved the purpose of their lives.
(72) O wise one, what could you obtain greater than this—that even Lakṣmī herself bears the earth as a gift in comparison to it?
Worship the lotus feet of the Supreme Lord, which are the source of Kedāra, pearls, and great medicinal herbs. (73)

May the lotus-feet of Him whose garment is the quarters of space perfume the casket of my heart with abundant divine fragrances, which are intent upon dispelling the various fetters of hope, afflictions, and evil latent impressions.
[May they perfume it] with one who is auspicious, possessing a graceful and variegated gait, swift, knowing all gestures, sinless, and enriched with the marks of steadfastness.
O Enemy of Smara, mount the horse of the mind and do not wander further; you have already mounted the bull of all the worlds.
75 Devotion dwelling upon the lotus-feet of Maheśa brings forth a rain of satisfaction like a bank of clouds.
The entire life of that person whose lake-like mind is completely filled is fruitful, and nothing else is so. 76

The intellect, fixed upon the lotus of the Lord’s sound like a wife longing for her husband, ever remembers Him; as if deluded by the constant recollection, visualization, and glorification of His true nature, it meditates through the chanting of the Śiva-mantra. (77) It relies upon a friend who is humble and instructed in the rules of proper service.
O Lord, uplift this intellect of mine with Your supreme quality, as one might support a newlywed bride.
O Śambhu, Your foot is capable of treading upon the lotus-petals of the minds of eternal yogis; how then could it cause a wound to the chest-panels of the hard Indra?
Alas, my mind reflects thus: Your pair of feet is exceedingly soft; O Lord, bring them within the range of my vision so that I may massage them with my hand.
This Mind shall take birth; its nature is hard, and it will dance upon that [Mind]. Therefore, for my protection, you have long practiced placing your delicate footsteps upon the peaks of mountains.
Otherwise, O Śambhu, why would your dancing be performed mostly upon stone slabs—within divine mansions, on flower-couches, or upon sacrificial altars?

He who, with his mind joyfully dedicated to you, attains such a state for some time through the worship of your lotus feet as Umā and Maheśvara, for some time through meditations and absorptions, for some time through prostrations, for some time through listening to your stories, for some time through glances, and for some time through hymns of praise— he is indeed liberated while living.
O Lord of Āryā, Hari assumed various forms such as being an arrow, a bull with half his body, a wife, a flute-player, a friend, and a drummer;
he even offered his eyes at Your feet as a portion of his own body. Indeed, he alone is the most worshipful among the worshipful; for if not he, who else could be superior?
(82) There is no doubt that for those subject to birth and death, there is not even a fraction of happiness to be gained by serving other deities.

Those who worship the unborn Lord Śambhu, whose nature is immortality, indeed attain supreme bliss in this world; they are truly blessed. (83) O Śiva, for the sake of your proximity through service, I shall offer my daughter of intellect, who is pre-eminent in virtue, to Gaurī.
O Friend of all worlds, O Ocean of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, take up residence forever within the temple of my compassionate heart. (84)

O Moon-crested Lord, tell me how I may arrange for you the primary offerings of food, flowers, ornaments, and garments; for I am neither skilled at crossing the ocean nor an expert hunter in the forest, nor am I greedy.
How can we perform worship when the abundance of ritual materials has not been prepared? I have attained neither the state of a bird, which is difficult to reach, nor even that of an insect.
O Lord, Umā’s father did not recognize the sprout-like foot upon his head; nor was it truly known by Hari, who had assumed that very form as the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Poison is my food, the serpent is my necklace, the elephant hide is my garment, and the great bull is my vehicle;
what else will you give me, O Śambhu? Give me only devotion to your lotus feet.
(87) When he had built the bridge across the ocean and held the lord of mountains beneath his palm—
O Bhavānī, at that time, having bypassed the Lotus-born Brahmā, you were capable of [only] the worship, praise, and meditation upon Śiva.
(88) O Lord, you were not satisfied by prostrations, hymns of praise, ritual procedures of worship, meditations, or absorptions;
tell me, how then do you act so as to bring pleasure to you with bows, clubs, or stones? (89)
I speak of the conduct of Śambhu with my speech, though I am unattached to the performance of worldly endeavors;
I serve the form of the Lord with my mind and I bow to Sadāśiva with my head.
(90) The primordial ignorance that had entered my heart has departed, and by your grace, wisdom has entered my heart.
O crest-jewel of kings, may I eternally serve your glorious lotus feet, which bring prosperity and are the vessel for liberation;

O Lord of Gaurī, uplift me here with your auspicious side-glances—me who drinks incessantly the essence of your life-story, while having cast far away all evils, harsh words, misfortune, suffering, false pride, and foul speech. (91–92)
May my heart dwell eternally upon the Lord of Girijā, the Great Radiance, whose head bears the crescent moon and whose neck is as delicate as a stalk of grain.
That tongue is truly blessed, those two eyes are blessed, and those two hands have fulfilled their purpose— those which speak of Bharga, behold Him, and ever worship and remember Him.

"O Lord of Bhavānī, my feet are exceedingly tender while your mind is extremely hard"—abandon such doubt; for on the mountain, your abode was likewise [firm]. Having firmly drawn [the mind] in with the goad of fortitude and the chain of devotion with sudden force...
Bind the elephant of your heart to the tethering post of the feet of the Destroyer of Cities with various [restraints].
This great elephant of the mind, intoxicated with passion, roams about on all sides with a bold gait.
Having seized it by means of the rope of devotion through the method of right conduct, I shall firmly lead it to the supreme state of Śiva.

[She is] endowed with every ornament, composed of simple words, virtuous in conduct, golden-hued, praised by the wise, possessed of the quality of aesthetic flavor (*sarasatva*), distinguished, and rich in auspicious marks.
O Lord, beloved of Gaurī, accept this auspicious maiden of poetry, who wears exquisite ornaments, who has attained discipline, whose lines of meaning shine forth, and who is truly beautiful.

O Supreme Śiva, ocean of compassion, was this appropriate for you? That you assumed the form of an animal with the intent of showing the head and feet of your own state to Hari and Brahmā, who wander upon heaven and earth exhausted by toil—O Śambhu, O Lord, tell me this; you are known before me.
Enough with this hymn; I shall speak no falsehood: even the gods, beginning with Viriñca, when engaged in the enumeration of those worthy of praise, know you to be their foremost.
O Śambhu, in the context of not investigating greatness, your own servants—like a mere heap of grain-husks—know you to be the fruit of the most supreme fruits.
Thus ends the Śivānandalaharī, among the works composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda.
